facts.en: As a British citizen or permanent resident you should: respect and obey the law; respect the rights of others (including their right to their own opinions); treat others with fairness; look after yourself and your family; look after the area in which you live and the environment; and pay taxes.

The five fundamental principles of British life are: democracy, the rule of law, individual liberty, tolerance of those with different faiths and beliefs, and participation in community life. Monarchy is NOT one of them.
The UK is made up of England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland. "Great Britain" refers only to England, Scotland and Wales (not Northern Ireland).
The Channel Islands (e.g. Jersey) and the Isle of Man are Crown dependencies: closely linked to the UK, with their own governments, but NOT part of the UK.
St Helena and the Falkland Islands are British overseas territories: linked to the UK but not part of it (and not part of Great Britain).
The UK is located in the north-west of Europe.
The first farmers came to Britain about 6,000 years ago, probably from south-east Europe.
Stonehenge, in Wiltshire (England), is a Stone Age monument built about 5,000 years ago.
The first coins minted in Britain were made in the Iron Age; some carried the names of Iron Age kings.
Julius Caesar led the first Roman invasion of Britain in 55 BC, which failed. The Romans conquered Britain under Emperor Claudius in AD 43.
Boudicca, queen of the Iceni tribe, led a revolt against the Romans (around AD 60).
Hadrian's Wall was built by the Romans (AD 122) across northern England to mark the northern boundary of their empire in Britain.
The Romans left Britain in AD 410. Tribes from northern Europe — the Jutes, Angles and Saxons — then settled in Britain.
The Vikings came from Denmark and Norway in the 9th and 10th centuries, using longships to trade and to raid. They invaded and settled in England.
King Alfred the Great united the Anglo-Saxon kingdoms to defeat the Vikings.
In 1066 William, Duke of Normandy (the Normans were descendants of Vikings who had settled in northern France), defeated King Harold at the Battle of Hastings — the Norman Conquest of England.
After the Norman Conquest a new ruling class, a new legal system and castles came to England. In the Middle Ages the nobility spoke Norman French while the peasants spoke Anglo-Saxon.
The Bayeux Tapestry is an embroidery that depicts the Norman Conquest of England in 1066.
The Tower of London was built by William the Conqueror after the Norman Conquest.
The Domesday Book (1086), commissioned by William the Conqueror, was a survey recording who owned land and what property existed in England.
In 1215 King John signed the Magna Carta, which limited the power of the King and established that no one — not even the King — is above the law.
In 1314 the Scots, led by Robert the Bruce, defeated the English at the Battle of Bannockburn, and Scotland remained independent.
The Hundred Years War between England and France (1337–1453) actually lasted 116 years.
The Black Death, a plague, arrived in England in 1348 and killed about one third of the population.
Geoffrey Chaucer wrote The Canterbury Tales, a series of poems about a group of people going on a pilgrimage to Canterbury.
The Wars of the Roses (1455–1485) were fought between the House of York and the House of Lancaster. Henry VII (Tudor) won and united the two houses.
Henry VIII had six wives; two were executed. His second wife, Anne Boleyn, was the mother of Elizabeth I.

The Reformation was a 16th-century movement that broke from the Catholic Church. Henry VIII established the Church of England (1534) because the Pope would not let him divorce his first wife, Catherine of Aragon.
During the Reformation, Henry VIII closed the Catholic monasteries and seized their wealth — the Dissolution of the Monasteries.
Elizabeth I (reigned 1558–1603), daughter of Henry VIII, was a Protestant queen. In 1588 the English defeated the Spanish Armada.
Mary, Queen of Scots was imprisoned by Elizabeth I for 20 years and then executed.
William Shakespeare was born in Stratford-upon-Avon (and went to Stratford Grammar School). He wrote plays including Hamlet and A Midsummer Night's Dream.
The Gunpowder Plot (1605) was a failed plot by Guy Fawkes and others to blow up Parliament and kill King James I.
The version of the Bible created under King James I (1611) is known as the Authorised Version, or King James Bible.
The Petition of Right (1628) confirmed that the King could not raise taxes without the consent of Parliament.
The English Civil War (1642–1651) was fought between Parliament and King Charles I over who held power. Charles I was executed.
After Charles I was executed in 1649, England was declared a republic (the Commonwealth) — the only period it was not ruled by a monarch.
Oliver Cromwell led the Parliamentarians in the Civil War and was given the title Lord Protector (1649–1658).
After his defeat in the Civil War, Charles II escaped to Europe, famously hiding in an oak tree (the "Royal Oak").
The Great Fire of London (1666), during the reign of Charles II, destroyed much of the city including St Paul's Cathedral.
Samuel Pepys was a 17th-century diarist who wrote about the Great Fire of London.
Sir Christopher Wren was the architect of St Paul's Cathedral, rebuilt after the Great Fire of London.
In the Glorious Revolution (1688) James II was peacefully replaced by William of Orange, establishing constitutional monarchy.
The Bill of Rights (1689) limited the power of the King and confirmed the rights of Parliament. It did NOT give anyone the right to vote.
The Act of Union 1707 united the Parliaments of England and Scotland, creating the Kingdom of Great Britain.
Sir Robert Walpole was the first Prime Minister (1721–1742).
In 1745 Bonnie Prince Charlie (Charles Edward Stuart) raised an army of Scottish Highland clansmen to try to regain the throne for the Stuarts; he was defeated at Culloden in 1746.
The Enlightenment was an 18th-century period when new ideas about politics, philosophy and science developed. Adam Smith developed ideas about economics.
Isaac Newton, born in Woolsthorpe, Lincolnshire, discovered the laws of gravity and motion. He was later Warden and then Master of the Royal Mint.
Robert Burns is Scotland's national poet; he wrote Auld Lang Syne. Burns Night is celebrated on 25th January.

The Industrial Revolution (18th–19th century) transformed Britain from an agricultural to an industrial economy with rapid urbanisation. Manufacturing became the biggest source of employment in the 18th century.
In 1776, 13 British colonies in North America declared their independence (the American War of Independence).
The Act of Union 1800 united Great Britain and Ireland, creating the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland.
At the Battle of Trafalgar (1805) Admiral Nelson commanded the British fleet, defeated the French and Spanish fleets, and was killed.
The Slave Trade Act 1807 abolished the slave trade in the British Empire; MP William Wilberforce led the campaign.
Sake Dean Mahomet opened Britain's first curry house in London (around 1810) and introduced shampooing to Britain.
At the Battle of Waterloo (1815) the Duke of Wellington ("the Iron Duke") defeated Napoleon — the last battle between Britain and France. Wellington later became Prime Minister.
Isambard Kingdom Brunel was a famous Victorian engineer who built bridges, tunnels, railways and ships.
The Great Reform Act 1832 extended the right to vote (to more of the middle classes).
The Chartists (mid-19th century) campaigned for political reform, including votes for all men.
The Irish famine (1840s) was caused by the failure of the potato crop; about a million people died and another million emigrated.
Florence Nightingale, a pioneer of modern nursing, improved hospital conditions during the Crimean War (1853–1856).
The Boer War (1899–1902) was fought in South Africa between the British and the Boer settlers.
The Suffragettes campaigned for women's right to vote; their leader was Emmeline Pankhurst.
The First World War (1914–1918) was triggered by the assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand and a complex system of alliances.
The Battle of the Somme (1916) was one of the bloodiest battles of WWI: about 20,000 British soldiers died on the first day.
The First World War ended at 11am on 11th November 1918.
In 1918 women over 30 were given the right to vote, in recognition of their contribution to the First World War.
In 1928 women were given the right to vote at 21, the same age as men.
In 1969 the voting age was lowered to 18 for both men and women.
Alexander Fleming, a Scottish scientist, discovered penicillin in 1928.
Sir Frank Whittle invented the jet engine in the 1930s.
The Second World War began in 1939 when Germany invaded Poland; Britain and France declared war on Germany.
Winston Churchill was Prime Minister during WWII (1940–1945, and again 1951–1955), an inspirational leader known for his speeches.
In 1940 British and Allied troops were evacuated from Dunkirk in France.
The Battle of Britain (1940) was the crucial aerial battle in which Britain defended itself against German air attacks, preventing invasion.
During the Blitz (1940–1941) Germany bombed British cities, especially London.
The Second World War ended in 1945: VE Day (Europe) on 8th May and VJ Day (Japan) on 15th August.
The Labour Party under Clement Attlee won the 1945 general election, despite Churchill's wartime popularity.
The National Health Service (NHS) was founded in 1948 by the Labour government (Aneurin Bevan): healthcare free at the point of use for all UK residents.
After WWII the Labour government built the Welfare State: a system providing social security, healthcare and education.
The Windrush Generation were Caribbean immigrants who came to the UK after WWII, from 1948 onwards.
Ireland became a republic in 1949.
Francis Crick (with James Watson) discovered the structure of DNA in 1953.
Edmund Hillary and Tenzing Norgay were the first to climb Mount Everest, in 1953, as part of a British expedition.
Roger Bannister was the first person to run a mile in under four minutes (1954).
David Hockney was an important contributor to the pop art movement of the 1960s.
Bobby Moore captained the England football team that won the World Cup in 1966.
Neil Armstrong was the first person to walk on the moon (1969, Apollo 11).
Concorde, the supersonic passenger aircraft, was developed by Britain and France.
The UK joined the European Community (now the EU) in 1973, and left the EU in 2020.
Margaret Thatcher was the first female Prime Minister (1979–1990) and the longest-serving PM of the 20th century.
Jayne Torvill and Christopher Dean won Olympic gold in ice dancing (1984).
The Berlin Wall fell in 1989, marking the end of the Cold War.
Tim Berners-Lee, a British computer scientist, invented the World Wide Web (1989).
The Good Friday Agreement (1998) brought peace to Northern Ireland after decades of conflict.
Alexander Graham Bell, born in Scotland, invented the telephone.
St George is the patron saint of England; St George's Day is 23rd April.
St Andrew is the patron saint of Scotland; St Andrew's Day is 30th November.
St Andrew was crucified on an X-shaped cross; the Scottish flag (the Saltire) is a white X-shaped cross on blue.
St David is the patron saint of Wales; St David's Day is 1st March.
St Patrick is the patron saint of Northern Ireland; St Patrick's Day is 17th March.
The Church of England is the established Protestant church of England, founded by Henry VIII. The Monarch is its head; the Archbishop of Canterbury is its spiritual leader.
The Church of Scotland is a Presbyterian church.
Wales and Northern Ireland do NOT have an established church; only England and Scotland do.
Easter takes place in March or April. Lent is the 40 days before Easter.
Boxing Day is 26th December, the day after Christmas Day, and is a public holiday.
Eid al-Fitr is a Muslim festival marking the end of Ramadan.
Eid ul Adha is an Islamic festival remembering Ibrahim's willingness to sacrifice his son.
Diwali, the Festival of Lights, is celebrated by Hindus and Sikhs.
Vaisakhi is a Sikh festival (April) marking the founding of the Khalsa.
Halloween is on 31st October.
Bonfire Night (Guy Fawkes Night) on 5th November commemorates the failure of the Gunpowder Plot of 1605.
Hogmanay is the Scottish name for New Year's Eve (31st December).
Remembrance Day (Armistice Day), 11th November, commemorates the end of WWI at 11am in 1918 and those who died in wars; people wear red poppies.
The Cenotaph is a war memorial in Whitehall, London, where the Remembrance Day ceremony is held.
Public holidays in the UK are called bank holidays: days when banks and many businesses are closed.
The national flower of England is the (Tudor) rose.
The national flower of Scotland is the thistle.
The national flower of Wales is the daffodil.
The national flower of Northern Ireland is the shamrock.
The Union Jack is red, white and blue, combining the crosses of England, Scotland and Ireland.
Welsh is spoken in Wales alongside English.
Gaelic is a Celtic language spoken in parts of Scotland and Ireland.
The UK currency is the pound sterling (£). Coins: 1p, 2p, 5p, 10p, 20p, 50p, £1 and £2 (there is no 25p coin).
The highest-value note in England is £50 (Scottish banks issue £100). Scotland and Northern Ireland have their own banknotes, which are valid everywhere in the UK.
The capital city of England (and the UK) is London.
The capital city of Scotland is Edinburgh.
The capital city of Wales is Cardiff.
The capital city of Northern Ireland is Belfast.
Big Ben is the clock tower bell at the Houses of Parliament in London.
Buckingham Palace is the Monarch's official residence in London.
The Tower of London is guarded by the Yeoman Warders, known as Beefeaters, who also give tours. The Crown Jewels (royal regalia used at coronations) are kept there.
Edinburgh Castle is in Edinburgh, Scotland.
The Giant's Causeway is in Northern Ireland: basalt columns formed by volcanic lava about 50 million years ago.
The Eden Project is a visitor attraction in Cornwall (south-west England) with giant greenhouse biomes.
Snowdonia National Park is in Wales; Snowdon is the highest mountain in Wales.
Ben Nevis, in Scotland, is the highest mountain in the UK (1,345 m).
The Lake District is the largest National Park in England.
Loch Lomond and the Trossachs National Park is in Scotland.
National Parks are areas of protected countryside; there are 15 in England, Wales and Scotland.
The Ashes is the famous cricket series played between England and Australia.
Wimbledon is an annual Grand Slam lawn tennis tournament held in London.
The Commonwealth Games is a multi-sport event held every four years for Commonwealth countries.
The BBC Proms is an annual eight-week classical music festival held at the Royal Albert Hall in London.
The Notting Hill Carnival is a Caribbean-influenced street festival held in London every August.
Glastonbury is a famous annual music festival held in Somerset, England.
London's West End is known as Theatreland.
The Tate galleries (Tate Britain and Tate Modern) are in London.
The National Galleries of Scotland are in Edinburgh.
The Turner Prize is an annual prize awarded to British visual artists.
J.M.W. Turner, a famous British landscape painter, painted 'The Fighting Temeraire'.
Henry Purcell and George Frideric Handel were two famous Baroque composers associated with Britain.
Richard Rogers was the architect of the Millennium Dome.
Harry Potter and James Bond are two of the highest-grossing film franchises produced in the UK.
British actors who have won Oscars include Colin Firth, Anthony Hopkins, Judi Dench, Kate Winslet and Tilda Swinton (Emily Watson has not).
The BBC is the largest broadcaster in the world and is independent of government.
The National Lottery (launched 1994) raises money for good causes including arts, sport and heritage.
Charles Dickens was a famous Victorian novelist who wrote 'A Christmas Carol' (also Oliver Twist, Great Expectations).
Jane Austen wrote 'Pride and Prejudice'.
Charlotte Brontë wrote 'Jane Eyre'.
Mary Shelley wrote 'Frankenstein'.
William Wordsworth wrote the poem 'The Daffodils'.
John Keats wrote the poem 'Ode to a Nightingale'.
Rudyard Kipling wrote the poem 'If' and 'The Jungle Book'.
The Monarch is the ceremonial head of state, signs legislation but acts on the advice of the Prime Minister, and must remain politically neutral.
The Monarch appoints the Prime Minister: by convention, the leader of the party with the most seats in the House of Commons.
At the State Opening of Parliament the Monarch opens the new session and reads the King's/Queen's Speech, which sets out the government's legislative programme (written by the PM).
The UK's constitutional institutions are the Monarchy, Parliament, the Prime Minister, the Cabinet, the judiciary, the police, the civil service and local government. The Armed Forces are NOT one.
Parliament has two houses: the House of Commons and the House of Lords.
The UK has 650 parliamentary constituencies, each electing one MP — so there are 650 MPs in the House of Commons.
The Speaker chairs debates in the House of Commons.
The House of Lords examines, revises and debates laws proposed by the House of Commons (it cannot reject financial bills).
Life peers are members of the House of Lords appointed for their lifetime only; the title cannot be inherited. Most members of the Lords are now life peers.
Hereditary peers inherit their title; only 92 remain in the House of Lords.
Several Church of England bishops (the Lords Spiritual, 26 in total) sit in the House of Lords.
An MP is elected by the voters of a constituency and represents everyone in it, helps to create new laws, and scrutinises the government.
A by-election is held when an MP dies or resigns.
Prime Minister's Questions (PMQs) is a weekly session (usually Wednesday) where MPs question the Prime Minister.
A hung parliament is when no single party wins enough seats for a majority.
The Prime Minister is head of government, leads the Cabinet and advises the Monarch. The official home of the PM is 10 Downing Street.
The Cabinet, chaired by the PM and made up of about 20 senior ministers, makes major government policy decisions.
The Shadow Cabinet is made up of senior opposition MPs, appointed by the Leader of the Opposition, who mirror Cabinet ministers and challenge the government.
The Home Secretary is responsible for crime, policing and immigration.
The Chancellor of the Exchequer is responsible for the country's finances and the economy.
The Lord Chancellor is responsible for the legal system and courts in England and Wales.
The Attorney General is the chief legal adviser to the government.
The Civil Service implements government policy and must remain politically neutral.
The Ombudsman investigates complaints about government departments and public services.
General elections are held at least every 5 years.
UK general elections use the 'first past the post' system: the candidate with the most votes in a constituency wins.
Proportional representation gives seats in proportion to votes received; it is used for the Northern Ireland Assembly (and the Scottish Parliament and Senedd).
A referendum is a public vote on a specific issue (e.g. the 2016 EU referendum).
To vote in a general election you must be 18 or over, a UK, Irish or Commonwealth citizen, and on the electoral register.
Before an election you are sent a poll card telling you where and when to vote; you use a ballot paper to vote.
By law, television and radio must give balanced political coverage before an election; newspapers are not bound by this rule.
The Electoral Commission oversees elections and maintains the electoral register.
Devolution is the transfer of power from central government to regional governments — Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland each have their own parliament or assembly.
The Scottish Parliament, in Edinburgh, has 129 members (MSPs).
The Welsh Parliament (Senedd Cymru, formerly the National Assembly for Wales), in Cardiff, has 60 members (MSs).
The Northern Ireland Assembly has 90 members (MLAs).
Defence, foreign affairs and immigration are NOT devolved — they are reserved to the UK government.

Towns, cities and rural areas are governed by democratically elected local councils, which provide services such as education, waste and housing. Councillors represent their community and decide on local services.
Habeas corpus is the legal principle that prevents people from being held in prison without trial.
Common law is law based on court decisions and precedents rather than legislation.
Presumption of innocence: a person is considered innocent until proven guilty.
Trial by jury: a panel of citizens decides whether the accused is guilty or innocent.
Jurors are aged 18 to 70 and are chosen randomly from the electoral register.
Carrying an offensive weapon is a criminal offence.
The small claims court deals with minor civil disputes.
The Supreme Court (established 2009) is the highest court in the UK.
Youth Courts in England and Wales (for those aged 10–17) are heard by specially trained magistrates or district judges; serious cases go to the Crown Court.
Solicitors give legal advice and represent clients; their charges are usually based on how much time they spend on a case.
Legal aid helps people who cannot afford to pay for legal advice.
Citizens Advice gives free, confidential advice on rights, legal matters and other issues.
The role of the police is to protect life and property, and to prevent and detect crime.
You can complain about the police by writing to the Chief Constable, at a police station, or to the independent complaints body (IOPC).
If you think someone is trying to persuade you to join an extremist or terrorist cause, contact your local police force.
Trade unions represent workers' interests and negotiate with employers.
The National Minimum Wage (introduced 1998) is the minimum hourly wage employers must pay.
The Human Rights Act 1998 incorporated the European Convention on Human Rights into UK law.
The Equality Act 2010 protects people from discrimination based on protected characteristics such as age, sex, race and religion.
The Equality and Human Rights Commission protects and promotes equality and human rights in Britain.
When walking your dog in a public place, it must wear a collar showing the name and address of the owner.
The National Citizen Service is a voluntary (not compulsory) programme for 16–17 year olds to develop skills and serve their community.
The National Trust is a charity that preserves important buildings, coastline and countryside in the UK.
Friends of the Earth is a charity that helps the environment.
Age UK is a charity that helps elderly people.
The NSPCC is the National Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Children.
The Commonwealth is an association of about 54 countries, mostly from the former British Empire.
The Council of Europe (47 members, separate from the EU) protects human rights and promotes democracy in Europe.
The European Convention on Human Rights protects fundamental rights and freedoms; it is enforced by the European Court of Human Rights in Strasbourg.
The United Nations was set up after the Second World War (1945) to prevent war and promote international peace.
The UN Security Council maintains international peace and security; the UK is one of its five permanent members.
The UN General Assembly is a forum where all member nations discuss and vote on international issues.
NATO (North Atlantic Treaty Organisation) was founded in 1949; the UK is a founding member committed to collective defence.
